query: For additively manufactured high-entropy-alloy components, what single intervention could improve dimensional precision and mechanical integrity while reducing fabrication-induced defects? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the current fabrication baseline, defines the processing and application conditions under which it should hold, identifies supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Optimizing process parameters such as laser power, scanning speed, and powder feed rate can improve dimensional precision and mechanical integrity while reducing fabrication-induced defects in additively manufactured high-entropy-alloy components.
generation.intervention: Optimization of laser power, scanning speed, and powder feed rate
generation.mechanism: Control of process parameters to minimize defects and optimize microstructure
generation.predicted_outcome: Improvement in dimensional precision and mechanical integrity by 10-20% relative to the current fabrication baseline
generation.baseline: Current fabrication baseline with standard process parameters
generation.boundary: Additive manufacturing process with optimized process parameters
generation.uncertainty: The exact relationship between process parameters and defect formation is not fully understood and may vary depending on the specific high-entropy alloy being used.

falsification_experiment.design: Experimental study with varying process parameters and measurement of dimensional precision and mechanical integrity
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the optimized process parameters do not result in a significant improvement (>= 5%) in dimensional precision and mechanical integrity compared to the current fabrication baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The objectives of this study are to investigate the effects of different processing parameters (laser power, scanning speed, and powder feed rate) on the quality of laser cladding AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy coatings (microhardness, dilution rate, and aspect ratio), to develop empirical models correlating these parameters with cladding quality, and to design a multi-objective optimization method for process parameters. This study aims to establish a foundation for the extensive application of laser cladding AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys in surface engineering, additive manufacturing, and remanufacturing, while providing insights relevant to process studies across various materials and additive manufacturing technologies. The research approach adopted in this study involves the following: orthogonal experiments were initially conducted on single-pass laser cladding of AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy to investigate the variations in cladding quality under different laser cladding process parameters. Subsequently, the data from the orthogonal experiments were then analyzed to assess the impact of various process parameters on the cladding quality evaluation indexes using the gray cor

The article comprehensively employs methods such as orthogonal experiments, gray relational analysis, multiple linear regression, multi-objective optimization design based on the NSGA-II algorithm, and finite element numerical simulation based on ANSYS Workbench to analyze the laser cladding process of AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy. Firstly, 16 groups of single-pass AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy coatings were prepared on the surface of H13 steel using YLS-4000-KC coaxial powder feeding laser cladding equipment. The macroscopic quality of the single pass cladding was good, the surface roughness was low, and there were no obvious defects such as cracks and wrinkles, which proves the feasibility of the laser cladding technology of AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys, and it also provides the basis for subsequent research. Secondly, gray correlation analysis of the data obtained from the orthogonal experiments shows that the powder feed rate exerts the most significant influence on microhardness, while laser power has the greatest impact on dilution rate, and scanning speed predominantly affects aspect ratio during the AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy laser cladding process.

Additive manufacturing (AM) is rapidly emerging as a pivotal technology for industrial part production due to its ability to create intricate shapes through computer-assisted layer-by-layer part construction. In metal AM, a broad, ever-expanding technology landscape has emerged with varying degrees of adoption in industry. While various AM technologies exist, liquid-mediated metal AM, notably Laser Powder Bed Fusion (L-PBF), has garnered significant interest in industry and academia due to its potential to produce high-quality parts. L-PBF’s quality relies on understanding the interplay between process parameters, material properties, and solidification conditions. Traditional alloy design primarily targets specific manufacturing routes and often overlooks the unique demands of additive manufacturing (AM). In AM, designing alloys requires optimizing both chemistry and processing conditions simultaneously to minimize defects and enhance reliability. Conventional approaches first focus on achieving target properties and then on developing scalable processing methods.
